head.citation-title: Effect of installation-induced damage on the pull-out capacity of interlocking joints in PHC pipe piles
head.abstracts: © 2026 Institution of Structural Engineers. Published by Elsevier Ltd. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.This study investigates the axial tensile behavior of interlocking mechanical connections in prestressed high-strength concrete (PHC) pipe piles, focusing on the often-overlooked effects of installation-induced damage. Full-scale axial pull-out tests were conducted on two PHC-600-B-130 pipe pile specimens with interlocking joints. The results revealed that installation damage significantly compromised joint integrity,with failure occurring exclusively via pull-out of the connecting pins, accompanied by thread stripping, at loads reaching only 60.0%–70.0% of the pile's design tensile capacity, and merely 51.0%–59.5% of the ultimate joint capacity without considering installation damage, while the concrete pile body remained intact. To further understand the underlying mechanisms, a detailed finite element analysis was performed, simulating both the push-in installation process and the subsequent tensile loading. The simulation successfully replicated the experimentally observed failure modes, identifying severe stress concentrations at the peripheral threads of the connecting block and the final thread of the pin. Based on these insights, two geometrical improvements were proposed and evaluated numerically. Modifying the thread to a non-tapered geometry increased the ultimate load by a factor of 1.44. Introducing a chamfer at the thread edge of the connecting block effectively mitigated stress concentrations and enhanced the load-bearing capacity of the joint. As the chamfer angle decreases, the ultimate load increases accordingly. When a 42.8° chamfer was applied, the ultimate load increased by a factor of 4.46.
